title: Thai grammar
variety: Central Thai (standard Thai, as spoken in Bangkok)
about: From your very first conversation to everyday Thai, one short lesson at a time. Each lesson gives you something you can say straight away, then the grammar that makes it work. You don't need to know any grammar: each grammar word is explained when you first need it. Every example is everyday Central Thai, in Thai script with a reading in Latin letters that shows the tones.

blocks.p: Listen to the end of each line. Nit always finishes with {{ค่ะ|kâ}}, Tom with {{ครับ|kráp}}. These little words have no meaning of their own: they make what you say polite and friendly, and Thais add them to almost every sentence when they talk to someone they don't know well.

blocks.means: a small word that changes how a sentence sounds (polite, friendly, a question) rather than what it says. Thai puts them at the end of the sentence: {{ครับ|kráp}}, {{ค่ะ|kâ}}.

blocks.p: **The speaker decides.** Which one you use depends on **who is speaking**, not on who you're talking to. A man says {{ครับ|kráp}}, to everyone. A woman says {{ค่ะ|kâ}}, and in a question she changes it to {{คะ|ká}}.

table: in a statement or an answer
on its own: “yes, OK, I'm listening”

blocks.p: **Tones.** In Thai the pitch of your voice is part of the word: {{ค่ะ|kâ}} and {{คะ|ká}} are different words only because of their tone. The reading shows the tone with a mark over the vowel: **a** (no mark) mid, level; **à** low; **â** falling, like a firm “No.”; **á** high; **ǎ** rising, like a surprised “Huh?”.

blocks.means: a short word that stands for a person or a thing: I, you, he, she, it.

blocks.p: **“I” for a man, “I” for a woman.** A man says {{ผม|pǒm}}, a woman says {{ฉัน|chǎn}} (in formal speech, {{ดิฉัน|dì-chǎn}}). It goes with the end word: {{ผม…ครับ|pǒm … kráp}}, {{ฉัน…ค่ะ|chǎn … kâ}}.

**“You”.** The polite “you” is {{คุณ|kun}}. It also goes before a name, like “Mr” or “Ms”: {{คุณนิด|kun nít}}. Thais often say the person's name where English says “you”: {{คุณทอมมาจากไหนคะ|kun tɔm maa jàak nǎi ká}} is, word for word, “Mr Tom comes from where?”.

**No “is”.** {{ชื่อ|chʉ̂ʉ}} means “to be called”, so {{ผมชื่อทอม|pǒm chʉ̂ʉ tɔm}} (“I am-called Tom”) needs nothing else. {{มาจาก|maa jàak}} is “come from”: {{ผมมาจากอเมริกา|pǒm maa jàak à-mee-rí-gaa}} “I come from America”.

blocks.means: a word that asks for a piece of information: what, where, who, when.

blocks.p: **Asking.** The question word goes where the answer will go, at the end: {{คุณชื่ออะไร|kun chʉ̂ʉ à-rai}} “you are-called what?”, {{มาจากไหน|maa jàak nǎi}} “come from where?”. To answer, put your answer in its place.

table: {{คุณชื่ออะไร|kun chʉ̂ʉ à-rai}} What's your name?
{{ผมชื่อทอม|pǒm chʉ̂ʉ tɔm}} My name is Tom.
{{คุณมาจากไหน|kun maa jàak nǎi}} Where are you from?
{{ฉันมาจากเชียงใหม่|chǎn maa jàak chiiang-mài}} I'm from Chiang Mai.

blocks.p: **Leaving out “I”.** Once it's clear who you're talking about, Thai drops the pronoun: {{ชื่อทอมครับ|chʉ̂ʉ tɔm kráp}} “(I'm) Tom.” This is normal and polite. And {{แล้ว…ล่ะ|lɛ́ɛo … lâ}} turns the question round: {{แล้วคุณล่ะ|lɛ́ɛo kun lâ}} “and you?”.

blocks.tip: **Reading the vowels.** A doubled letter is a long vowel ({{มา|maa}}, a long “ah”). **ɛ** is the e of “bed”, **ɔ** the aw of “law”, **ʉ** an “oo” said with the lips spread, **ə** the u of “fur”. **bp** and **dt** are a p and a t with no puff of air (as in “spin”, “stop”); plain **p**, **t** and **k** have the puff, as in “pin”.

blocks.means: a word for a person, a thing or a place: teacher, coffee, Bangkok.
a word for an action or a state: go, eat, teach, be.

blocks.p: **เป็น, “to be”.** To say what someone *is* (a job, a nationality, a role), put the verb {{เป็น|bpen}} between the person and the noun: {{ผมเป็นหมอ|pǒm bpen mɔ̌ɔ}} “I am doctor”. Thai has no word for “a”: the noun alone is enough.

**Nationalities.** “A Thai” is {{คนไทย|kon tai}}, literally “person Thai”: {{คน|kon}} “person”, then the country. {{คนอังกฤษ|kon ang-grìt}} “English”, {{คนญี่ปุ่น|kon yîi-bpùn}} “Japanese”, {{คนอเมริกัน|kon à-mee-rí-gan}} “American”. A language is {{ภาษา|paa-sǎa}} “language” + the country: {{ภาษาไทย|paa-sǎa tai}}, {{ภาษาอังกฤษ|paa-sǎa ang-grìt}}.

**Not.** To say what someone is *not*, use {{ไม่ใช่|mâi châi}} in place of {{เป็น|bpen}}: {{ผมไม่ใช่หมอ|pǒm mâi-châi mɔ̌ɔ}} “I'm not a doctor”. {{ไม่ได้เป็น|mâi dâai bpen}} means the same: {{ผมไม่ได้เป็นหมอ|pǒm mâi dâai bpen mɔ̌ɔ}}. On its own, {{ไม่ใช่|mâi châi}} is “no, that's not right”.

**Asking someone's job.** {{คุณทำงานอะไร|kun tam-ngaan à-rai}} “you work what?”: {{ทำงาน|tam-ngaan}} is “to work”. You can answer with {{เป็น|bpen}} and a job, or say where you work: {{ผมทำงานที่ธนาคาร|pǒm tam-ngaan tîi tá-naa-kaan}} “I work at a bank”.

blocks.means: a word that describes a person or a thing: big, hot, delicious, tired.

blocks.p: **No “is” with describing words.** In Thai a word like “delicious”, “big” or “tired” works like a verb all by itself: {{อร่อย|à-rɔ̀i}} means “to be delicious”. So {{อาหารอร่อย|aa-hǎan à-rɔ̀i}} is a whole sentence: “the food is delicious”. Never put {{เป็น|bpen}} before an adjective.

**After the noun.** The describing word comes after the thing it describes: {{อาหารไทย|aa-hǎan tai}} “food Thai” = Thai food, {{ห้องใหญ่|hɔ̂ng yài}} “room big” = a big room. The same words can also be a sentence, “the room is big”: the situation tells you which.
**Very, a little, not.** {{มาก|mâak}} “very, a lot” and {{นิดหน่อย|nít-nɔ̀i}} “a little” go after the adjective. {{ไม่|mâi}} “not” goes before it.

blocks.p: **Asking.** Take any statement and put {{ไหม|mǎi}} at the end: it becomes a yes/no question. Nothing else changes: no new word order, no “do”. {{คุณชอบกาแฟ|kun chɔ̂ɔp gaa-fɛɛ}} “you like coffee” → {{คุณชอบกาแฟไหม|kun chɔ̂ɔp gaa-fɛɛ mǎi}} “do you like coffee?”. The end word comes last: {{…ไหมครับ|… mǎi kráp}}, {{…ไหมคะ|… mǎi ká}}.

**Answering.** Thai has no all-purpose “yes”. You answer with the verb or the adjective of the question: {{ชอบ|chɔ̂ɔp}} “(I) like (it)”, or {{ไม่ชอบ|mâi chɔ̂ɔp}} “(I) don't like (it)”. Then your end word.

table: {{หิวไหม|hǐu mǎi}} Are you hungry?
{{ชอบไหม|chɔ̂ɔp mǎi}} Do you like it?
{{เผ็ดไหม|pèt mǎi}} Is it spicy?

blocks.p: **…, right?** To check something you think is true, end with {{ใช่ไหม|châi mǎi}}: {{คุณเป็นคนไทยใช่ไหม|kun bpen kon tai châi mǎi}} “you're Thai, right?”. Now the answer is {{ใช่|châi}} “yes, that's right” or {{ไม่ใช่|mâi châi}} “no”.

blocks.p: **This, that, that over there.** On their own, pointing: {{นี่|nîi}} “this (here, near me)”, {{นั่น|nân}} “that (near you)”, {{โน่น|nôon}} “that (over there, far from us both)”. All three have a falling tone.

**คือ, “is”.** {{นี่คืออะไร|nîi kʉʉ à-rai}} is “this is what?”, and the answer puts the name in place of {{อะไร|à-rai}}: {{นี่คือทุเรียน|nîi kʉʉ tú-riian}} “this is durian”. In quick speech {{คือ|kʉʉ}} is often left out: {{นั่นอะไร|nân à-rai}}, {{นั่นมังคุด|nân mang-kút}}. Or just say the name: {{ทุเรียนค่ะ|tú-riian kâ}}.

**เป็น or คือ?** Both come before a noun. {{เป็น|bpen}} says what group or job someone belongs to: {{ฉันเป็นครู|chǎn bpen kruu}} “I'm a teacher (one of many)”. {{คือ|kʉʉ}} says *which one* something is, or what it means: {{นี่คือบ้านของฉัน|nîi kʉʉ bâan kɔ̌ɔng chǎn}} “this is my house”.
**What's it called?** {{เรียกว่า|rîiak wâa}} means “is called”: {{ภาษาไทยเรียกว่าอะไร|paa-sǎa tai rîiak wâa à-rai}} “in Thai, (it's) called what?”. The answer: {{เรียกว่า…|rîiak wâa …}} and the word.

lessons.summary: Introduce people and talk about them: he, she, we, they, and the Thai way of calling people by name or by a family word.

blocks.p: **He and she are one word.** {{เขา|kǎo}} means “he” *and* “she” (and “him”, “her”). Anna uses it for Somchai and for Fon: who is meant is clear from the situation.

**We, they, it.** {{เรา|rao}} is “we, us”. For “they”, add {{พวก|pûuak}} “group”: {{พวกเขา|pûuak-kǎo}} (or just {{เขา|kǎo}} again). {{มัน|man}} is “it”, for animals and things; but for things Thai usually says nothing at all: {{อร่อยมาก|à-rɔ̀i mâak}} “(it's) delicious”.

table: animals and things; often left out

blocks.p: **Names and family words.** Thais often use a name where English says “you” or “he”: {{คุณนิดไปไหนคะ|kun nít bpai nǎi ká}} “where is Nit going?”, asked to Nit herself. With friends and people about your age, Thais use family words: {{พี่|pîi}} “older brother or sister” for someone a little older, {{น้อง|nɔ́ɔng}} “younger brother or sister” for someone younger. Even with a waiter or a shop assistant: {{พี่ครับ|pîi kráp}} “excuse me!” (to someone a bit older).

blocks.p: **ขอ, “may I have”.** {{ขอ|kɔ̌ɔ}} and the thing you want is the everyday way to ask for something: {{ขอน้ำ|kɔ̌ɔ náam}} “water, please”. It's polite as it is; {{หน่อย|nɔ̀i}} “a little” at the end makes it softer, a bit like “please”.

**เอา, “I'll take”.** When you choose between things, {{เอา|ao}} “take” is the usual word: {{เอากาแฟร้อน|ao gaa-fɛɛ rɔ́ɔn}} “(I'll take) a hot coffee”. Staff ask {{รับอะไรดี|ráp à-rai dii}} “what will you have?”, or {{เอาอะไร|ao à-rai}} in a street stall.

**Can I…? Could you…?** Put {{ได้ไหม|dâai mǎi}} “is that possible?” after what you'd like: {{ขอเมนูได้ไหม|kɔ̌ɔ mee-nuu dâai mǎi}} “could I have the menu?”, {{จ่ายด้วยบัตรได้ไหม|jàai dûai bàt dâai mǎi}} “can I pay by card?”. The answer is {{ได้|dâai}} “yes, you can” or {{ไม่ได้|mâi dâai}} “no, you can't”.

blocks.p: **Please do…** {{ช่วย|chûai}} means “help”. Put it before a verb and {{หน่อย|nɔ̀i}} after, and you have a polite request: {{ช่วยพูดอีกทีหน่อย|chûai pûut ìik tii nɔ̀i}} “please say it again”. Add {{ได้ไหม|dâai mǎi}} to make it a question, and it's softer still: {{ช่วยพูดช้าๆ หน่อยได้ไหม|chûai pûut cháa-cháa nɔ̀i dâai mǎi}} “could you speak slowly?”.
**Doubled words.** Saying an adjective twice makes it gentler, “nice and…”: {{ช้าๆ|cháa-cháa}} “nice and slow”, {{ดีๆ|dii-dii}} “nicely, properly”. In writing, the second one is the little mark ๆ.

**Not understanding.** {{เข้าใจ|kâo-jai}} is “understand”: {{ไม่เข้าใจ|mâi kâo-jai}} “I don't understand”, {{เข้าใจแล้ว|kâo-jai lɛ́ɛo}} “I get it now”. To ask what a word means, say the word, then {{แปลว่าอะไร|bplɛɛ wâa à-rai}} “translates as what?”.

blocks.means: a counting word that comes after a number and shows what kind of thing is counted, like “cups” in “two cups of tea”. Thai uses one with every number.

blocks.p: **A counting word for everything.** English counts a few things with a word in between: “two cups of tea”, “three pieces of paper”. Thai does it with everything: the noun, the number, then the **classifier**: {{กาแฟสองแก้ว|gaa-fɛɛ sɔ̌ɔng gɛ̂ɛo}} “coffee two glass”, {{เพื่อนสามคน|pʉ̂ʉan sǎam kon}} “friend three person”.

**Bigger numbers** are built like English: 12 is {{สิบสอง|sìp-sɔ̌ɔng}} “ten-two”, 30 {{สามสิบ|sǎam-sìp}} “three-ten”. Two changes: 20 is {{ยี่สิบ|yîi-sìp}}, and a 1 at the end of a bigger number is {{เอ็ด|èt}}: 11 {{สิบเอ็ด|sìp-èt}}, 21 {{ยี่สิบเอ็ด|yîi-sìp-èt}}. 100 is {{ร้อย|rɔ́ɔi}}, 1,000 {{พัน|pan}}.

blocks.p: **One, and how many.** With {{หนึ่ง|nʉ̀ng}} “one”, the number can also go after the classifier: {{กาแฟแก้วหนึ่ง|gaa-fɛɛ gɛ̂ɛo nʉ̀ng}} is as natural as {{กาแฟหนึ่งแก้ว|gaa-fɛɛ nʉ̀ng gɛ̂ɛo}}. “How many?” is {{กี่|gìi}} + the classifier: {{กี่คน|gìi kon}} “how many people?”. In restaurants staff say {{กี่ท่าน|gìi tâan}}: {{ท่าน|tâan}} is a very polite classifier for people.

blocks.p: **This shirt, that car.** After a noun, “this” is {{นี้|níi}} and “that” is {{นั้น|nán}}, both high tone, and the classifier goes in between: {{เสื้อตัวนี้|sʉ̂ʉa dtuua níi}} “shirt (classifier) this” = this shirt, {{รถคันนั้น|rót kan nán}} “that car”. ({{นี่|nîi}} and {{นั่น|nân}}, falling, from lesson 6, stand on their own.)

table: {{เสื้อตัวนี้|sʉ̂ʉa dtuua níi}}
{{เสื้อตัวนั้น|sʉ̂ʉa dtuua nán}}
{{กระเป๋าใบนี้|grà-bpǎo bai níi}}
{{กระเป๋าใบนั้น|grà-bpǎo bai nán}}
{{หนังสือเล่มนี้|nǎng-sʉ̌ʉ lêm níi}}
{{หนังสือเล่มนั้น|nǎng-sʉ̌ʉ lêm nán}}

blocks.p: **This one, that one.** Leave the noun out and keep the classifier: {{ตัวนี้|dtuua níi}} “this one” (a shirt), {{ใบนั้น|bai nán}} “that one” (a bag). If you don't know the classifier, {{อันนี้|an níi}} “this one” works for almost any object.

**How much?** {{เท่าไหร่|tâo-rài}} “how much” goes at the end, where the price will go: {{อันนี้เท่าไหร่|an níi tâo-rài}} “this one, how much?”. Prices are in {{บาท|bàat}}, baht. To bargain: {{ลดได้ไหม|lót dâai mǎi}} “can you lower it?”. And {{จัง|jang}} after an adjective means “so”: {{แพงจัง|pɛɛng jang}} “so expensive!”.

lessons.summary: Ask a hotel whether there's a room, say what you have, and what there isn't: all with one verb, {{มี|mii}}.

blocks.p: **One verb for “have” and “there is”.** {{มี|mii}} means “have”: {{ผมมีพี่สาว|pǒm mii pîi sǎao}} “I have an older sister”. With no one before it, it means “there is, there are”: {{มีร้านอาหาร|mii ráan aa-hǎan}} “there are restaurants”.
**Not, and asking.** {{ไม่มี|mâi mii}} is “don't have, there isn't”. {{มี…ไหม|mii … mǎi}} asks “is there…?, do you have…?”, and the answer is the verb: {{มี|mii}} or {{ไม่มี|mâi mii}}.

blocks.p: **How many?** {{มี|mii}}, the noun, then {{กี่|gìi}} and the classifier: {{คุณมีพี่น้องกี่คน|kun mii pîi nɔ́ɔng gìi kon}} “how many brothers and sisters do you have?”. Answer: {{มีสองคน|mii sɔ̌ɔng kon}} “I have two”.

lessons.summary: Ask where the restroom is, and say where things and people are: in, on, under, next to, near.
lessons.topic: {{อยู่|yùu}} “be (somewhere)”; {{ที่ไหน|tîi-nǎi}}; {{ใน|nai}}, {{บน|bon}}, {{ใต้|dtâai}}, {{ข้าง|kâang}}, {{หน้า|nâa}}, {{หลัง|lǎng}}, {{ใกล้|glâi}}, {{ตรงข้าม|dtrong-kâam}}

goal.r: hɔ̂ng-náam yùu tîi-nǎi ká
goal.tr: Where's the restroom?

dialog.tr: It's on the second floor, next to the café.

blocks.p: **อยู่, “to be (somewhere)”.** For *where* something is, Thai has a third “be”: {{อยู่|yùu}}. {{ห้องน้ำอยู่ชั้นสอง|hɔ̂ng-náam yùu chán sɔ̌ɔng}} “the restroom is (on) floor two”. Not {{เป็น|bpen}}, not {{คือ|kʉʉ}}: those say what a thing is; {{อยู่|yùu}} says where it is.

**Where?** {{ที่ไหน|tîi-nǎi}} “at which place” (or just {{ไหน|nǎi}}) goes at the end, where the answer will go: {{คุณอยู่ที่ไหน|kun yùu tîi-nǎi}} “where are you?”, {{บ้านคุณอยู่ไหน|bâan kun yùu nǎi}} “where's your house?”.

blocks.means: a word that shows where something is, or how two things are linked: in, on, under, next to.

table: {{ในกระเป๋า|nai grà-bpǎo}} in the bag
{{บนโต๊ะ|bon dtó}} on the table
{{ใต้เตียง|dtâai dtiiang}} under the bed
{{ข้างธนาคาร|kâang tá-naa-kaan}} next to the bank
{{หน้าโรงแรม|nâa roong-rɛɛm}} in front of the hotel
{{หลังบ้าน|lǎng bâan}} behind the house
{{ใกล้ทะเล|glâi tá-lee}} near the sea
{{ตรงข้ามตลาด|dtrong-kâam dtà-làat}} across from the market

blocks.p: **Here, there.** {{ที่นี่|tîi-nîi}} “here”, {{ที่นั่น|tîi-nân}} “there”, {{ที่โน่น|tîi-nôon}} “over there”: {{ที่|tîi}} “place” and the pointing words you know. And {{ข้างบน|kâang-bon}} “upstairs”, {{ข้างล่าง|kâang-lâang}} “downstairs”.

blocks.p: **No “to”.** {{ไป|bpai}} “go” and {{มา|maa}} “come” take the place straight after them: {{ไปตลาด|bpai dtà-làat}} “go (to the) market”, {{มาบ้านฉัน|maa bâan chǎn}} “come (to) my house”. “Go where?” is {{ไปไหน|bpai nǎi}}.

**How?** {{ยังไง|yang-ngai}} “how” goes at the end: {{ไปสนามบินยังไง|bpai sà-nǎam bin yang ngai}} “go (to the) airport how?”. The answer says the way: {{นั่งรถไฟฟ้าไป|nâng rót-fai-fáa bpai}} “take the Skytrain”, literally “sit Skytrain go”.

**Telling someone what to do.** A verb on its own is a request or an instruction: {{ตรงไป|dtrong bpai}} “go straight”, {{จอด|jɔ̀ɔt}} “stop (the car)”. Keep {{ครับ|kráp}} / {{ค่ะ|kâ}} to be polite, and add {{เลย|ləəi}} for “right away, go ahead”: {{จอดตรงนี้เลย|jɔ̀ɔt dtrong níi ləəi}} “stop right here”.

table: {{เลี้ยวซ้าย|líao sáai}}

blocks.p: **Up, down, in, out.** {{ขึ้น|kʉ̂n}} “go up, get on”, {{ลง|long}} “go down, get off”, {{เข้า|kâo}} “go in”, {{ออก|ɔ̀ɔk}} “go out” often team up with {{ไป|bpai}} or {{มา|maa}}, which say whether the move is away from the speaker or toward them: {{ขึ้นไป|kʉ̂n bpai}} “go up (there)”, {{เข้ามา|kâo maa}} “come in (here)”.

blocks.p: **อยาก + a verb.** {{อยาก|yàak}} “want (to)” goes straight before the verb, with nothing in between: {{อยากไป|yàak bpai}} “want to go”, {{อยากกิน|yàak gin}} “want to eat”. There's no word for “to”.

**อยากได้ + a thing.** For a *thing* you'd like to have, say {{อยากได้|yàak dâai}} “want to get”: {{ฉันอยากได้โทรศัพท์ใหม่|chǎn yàak dâai too-rá-sàp mài}} “I'd like a new phone”. {{อยาก|yàak}} on its own needs a verb after it.

**Not, and asking.** {{ไม่อยาก|mâi yàak}} is “don't want to”. {{อยาก…ไหม|yàak … mǎi}} asks “do you want to…?”, and the question words work as always: {{อยากทำอะไร|yàak tam à-rai}} “what do you want to do?”, {{อยากไปไหน|yàak bpai nǎi}} “where do you want to go?”.

**ต้องการ.** {{ต้องการ|dtɔ̂ng-gaan}} “want, need” is formal: it's what you read on forms and hear in offices ({{ต้องการความช่วยเหลือไหม|dtɔ̂ng-gaan kwaam chûai lʉ̌ʉa mǎi}} “do you need help?”). In conversation, use {{อยาก|yàak}}.

blocks.means: the form of a verb that shows when something happens: English “eat, ate”. Thai verbs have no tenses.

blocks.p: **Verbs never change.** A Thai verb has one form, whoever does it and whenever: {{ผมกิน|pǒm gin}} “I eat”, {{เขากิน|kǎo gin}} “she eats”, {{เมื่อวานเรากิน|mʉ̂ʉa-waan rao gin}} “yesterday we ate”. No endings to learn: {{กิน|gin}} is always {{กิน|gin}}.

**Time words tell when.** Words like {{ทุกวัน|túk wan}} “every day” or {{ตอนเช้า|dtɔɔn cháao}} “in the morning” go at the start or at the end of the sentence, not in the middle: {{ทุกวันผมกินข้าวเช้า|túk wan pǒm gin kâao cháao}} or {{ผมกินข้าวเช้าทุกวัน|pǒm gin kâao cháao túk wan}}, both “I have breakfast every day”.

blocks.p: **How often.** {{ปกติ|bpòk-gà-dtì}} “usually” and {{บางที|baang-tii}} “sometimes” start the sentence. {{บ่อย|bɔ̀i}} “often” goes at the end: {{ผมไปตลาดบ่อย|pǒm bpai dtà-làat bɔ̀i}} “I go to the market often”. {{ไม่ค่อย|mâi kɔ̂i}} “not much, hardly” goes before the verb: {{ฉันไม่ค่อยดูทีวี|chǎn mâi kɔ̂i duu tii-wii}} “I don't watch TV much”.
**ก็.** In {{บางทีผมก็ดูทีวี|baang-tii pǒm gɔ̂ duu tii-wii}}, the little {{ก็|gɔ̂}} links the time word to the rest, a bit like “then”. Thais use it all the time, and you'll see it again.

lessons.title: Do two things in one sentence: go and buy, come and eat
lessons.summary: Put verbs one after another, the Thai way: “go buy coffee”, “walk to work”, “bring it here”.
lessons.topic: Verbs in a row ({{ไปซื้อ|bpai sʉ́ʉ}}, {{มากิน|maa gin}}, {{เดินไป|dəən bpai}}); {{ไป|bpai}} / {{มา|maa}} for direction; {{เอา…มา|ao … maa}} “bring”, {{เอา…ไป|ao … bpai}} “take”

goal.t: วันเสาร์ผมไปเล่นฟุตบอลกับเพื่อนครับ
goal.r: wan sǎo pǒm bpai lên fút-bɔn gàp pʉ̂ʉan kráp
goal.tr: On Saturdays I go and play soccer with friends.

dialog.r: tɔm, maa gin kâao tîi bâan mǎi ká
dialog.tr: Tom, would you like to come and eat at my place?

dialog.r: dâai kráp, dǐao pǒm ao kà-nǒm bpai kráp

dialog.tr: Thanks! You can walk over: the house is close.

dialog.tr: OK. I'll stop off and buy some ice first.

blocks.means: two or more verbs side by side for one person's actions, with no “and” or “to” between them: Thai {{ไปซื้อ|bpai sʉ́ʉ}} “go buy”.

blocks.p: **One verb after another.** Thai often puts two or three verbs side by side, with no “and” and no “to”: {{ไปซื้อกาแฟ|bpai sʉ́ʉ gaa-fɛɛ}} “go buy coffee”, {{มากินข้าว|maa gin kâao}} “come eat”. They come in the order things happen: first you go, then you buy.

table: {{ไปซื้อของ|bpai sʉ́ʉ kɔ̌ɔng}}
{{เดินไปโรงเรียน|dəən bpai roong-riian}}
{{นั่งรถเมล์ไป|nâng rót-mee bpai}}
{{กลับบ้านไปนอน|glàp bâan bpai nɔɔn}}

blocks.p: **ไป and มา show the direction.** After a verb of moving, {{ไป|bpai}} means away from the speaker and {{มา|maa}} toward the speaker: {{เดินไป|dəən bpai}} “walk (there)”, {{เดินมา|dəən maa}} “walk (here)”; {{วิ่งออกไป|wîng ɔ̀ɔk bpai}} “run out”, {{เข้ามา|kâo maa}} “come in”.
**Bring and take.** {{เอา|ao}} “take hold of”, the thing, then {{มา|maa}} or {{ไป|bpai}}: {{เอาน้ำมา|ao náam maa}} “bring the water (here)”, {{เอาร่มไป|ao rôm bpai}} “take an umbrella (with you)”.

ex.t: ฉันไปซื้อของที่ตลาดค่ะ

ex.tr: I'm going shopping at the market.

ex.t: เขาวิ่งออกไปข้างนอกค่ะ

lessons.title: Say what you like and don't like
lessons.summary: Say what you love, like, don't really like or can't stand, and what you prefer.
lessons.topic: {{ชอบ|chɔ̂ɔp}} + a thing or a verb; {{ชอบ…มาก|chɔ̂ɔp … mâak}}; {{ไม่ค่อยชอบ|mâi kɔ̂i chɔ̂ɔp}}; {{ไม่ชอบ…เลย|mâi chɔ̂ɔp … ləəi}}; {{ชอบ…มากกว่า|chɔ̂ɔp … mâak gwàa}}

goal.t: ฉันชอบกินอาหารเผ็ดค่ะ
goal.r: chǎn chɔ̂ɔp gin aa-hǎan pèt kâ
goal.tr: I like spicy food.

dialog.t: คุณชอบทำอะไรตอนว่างครับ
dialog.r: kun chɔ̂ɔp tam à-rai dtɔɔn wâang kráp
dialog.tr: What do you like doing in your free time?

dialog.t: ฉันชอบอ่านหนังสือค่ะ แล้วก็ชอบดูหนัง
dialog.r: chǎn chɔ̂ɔp àan nǎng-sʉ̌ʉ kâ, lɛ́ɛo-gɔ̂ chɔ̂ɔp duu nǎng
dialog.tr: I like reading. And I like watching movies.

dialog.t: ชอบหนังผีไหมครับ
dialog.r: chɔ̂ɔp nǎng pǐi mǎi kráp

dialog.t: ไม่ชอบเลยค่ะ กลัว ฉันชอบหนังตลกมากกว่า
dialog.r: mâi chɔ̂ɔp ləəi kâ, gluua, chǎn chɔ̂ɔp nǎng dtà-lòk mâak gwàa
dialog.tr: Not at all! They scare me. I prefer comedies.

blocks.p: **ชอบ + a thing, or a verb.** {{ชอบ|chɔ̂ɔp}} “like” takes a thing ({{ชอบกาแฟ|chɔ̂ɔp gaa-fɛɛ}} “like coffee”) or a verb straight after it ({{ชอบอ่านหนังสือ|chɔ̂ɔp àan nǎng-sʉ̌ʉ}} “like reading”). As with {{อยาก|yàak}}, there's nothing for “to” or “-ing”.

**How much.** {{มาก|mâak}} goes at the end: {{ชอบทะเลมาก|chɔ̂ɔp tá-lee mâak}} “I love the sea”. For less, {{ไม่ค่อยชอบ|mâi kɔ̂i chɔ̂ɔp}} “don't really like”; for none at all, {{ไม่ชอบ…เลย|mâi chɔ̂ɔp … ləəi}}: {{เลย|ləəi}} at the end of a negative means “at all”.

table: {{ไม่ค่อยชอบ|mâi kɔ̂i chɔ̂ɔp}}
{{ไม่ชอบเลย|mâi chɔ̂ɔp ləəi}}

blocks.p: **Prefer.** {{ชอบ…มากกว่า|chɔ̂ɔp … mâak gwàa}} “like … more (than)”: {{ฉันชอบชามากกว่ากาแฟ|chǎn chɔ̂ɔp chaa mâak-gwàa gaa-fɛɛ}} “I prefer tea to coffee”. {{กว่า|gwàa}} “than” comes back in the lesson on comparing.

**Asking.** {{ชอบ…ไหม|chɔ̂ɔp … mǎi}} “do you like…?”, {{ชอบอะไร|chɔ̂ɔp à-rai}} “what do you like?”, {{ชอบทำอะไร|chɔ̂ɔp tam à-rai}} “what do you like doing?”. After a noun, {{อะไร|à-rai}} means “which, what kind of”: {{ชอบกีฬาอะไร|chɔ̂ɔp gii-laa à-rai}} “what sports do you like?”.

ex.r: chǎn mâi chɔ̂ɔp aa-gàat rɔ́ɔn ləəi kâ

ex.t: คุณชอบกีฬาอะไรคะ

blocks.tip: {{ชอบ|chɔ̂ɔp}} is also how you tell someone you like them: {{ผมชอบคุณ|pǒm chɔ̂ɔp kun}} “I like you”. “Love” is {{รัก|rák}}.

lessons.summary: Ask for information with all the question words, and know where each one goes.
lessons.topic: The question word stays where the answer goes: {{อะไร|à-rai}}, {{ใคร|krai}}, {{ที่ไหน|tîi-nǎi}}, {{เมื่อไหร่|mʉ̂ʉa-rài}}, {{ทำไม|tam-mai}}, {{ยังไง|yang-ngai}}

blocks.p: **Where the answer goes.** In English the question word jumps to the front (“*Where* do you work?”). In Thai it stays where the answer will be: {{คุณทำงานที่ไหน|kun tam-ngaan tîi-nǎi}} “you work where?” → {{ผมทำงานที่ธนาคาร|pǒm tam-ngaan tîi tá-naa-kaan}} “I work at the bank”. Swap the question word for the answer, and you have your reply.

table: {{คุณกินอะไร|kun gin à-rai}} What are you eating?
{{เขาเป็นใคร|kǎo bpen krai}} Who is he?
{{คุณพักที่ไหน|kun pák tîi-nǎi}} Where are you staying?
{{คุณกลับเมื่อไหร่|kun glàp mʉ̂ʉa-rài}} When are you going back?
{{ทำไมไม่กิน|tam-mai mâi gin}} Why aren't you eating?
{{ไปยังไง|bpai yang-ngai}} How do you get there?
{{ค่าห้องเท่าไหร่|kâa hɔ̂ng tâo-rài}} How much is the room?

blocks.p: **Who did it?** When “who” is the one *doing* the action, {{ใคร|krai}} comes first, because that's where the answer goes: {{ใครสอนคุณ|krai sɔ̌ɔn kun}} “who teaches you?” → {{แฟนผมสอน|fɛɛn pǒm sɔ̌ɔn}} “my girlfriend teaches (me)”. Compare {{คุณสอนใคร|kun sɔ̌ɔn krai}} “who do you teach?”.
**Why.** {{ทำไม|tam-mai}} usually goes at the start: {{ทำไมมาสาย|tam-mai maa sǎai}} “why are you late?”. At the end ({{มาสายทำไม|maa sǎai tam-mai}}) it sounds annoyed, so keep it at the front.

**When.** {{เมื่อไหร่|mʉ̂ʉa-rài}} “when” goes at the end, and the answer is a time word: {{พรุ่งนี้|prûng-níi}} “tomorrow”, {{เดือนหน้า|dʉʉan nâa}} “next month”, {{เดือนที่แล้ว|dʉʉan tîi-lɛ́ɛo}} “last month”.

lessons.summary: Talk about your family, say whose things are, and ask someone's age.
lessons.topic: {{ของ|kɔ̌ɔng}} “of” (often left out: {{แม่ผม|mɛ̂ɛ pǒm}}); family words by age ({{พี่|pîi}} / {{น้อง|nɔ́ɔng}} + {{ชาย|chaai}} / {{สาว|sǎao}}); {{ของใคร|kɔ̌ɔng krai}}; {{อายุ|aa-yú}}

blocks.p: **Whose: ของ.** {{ของ|kɔ̌ɔng}} means “of, belonging to”, and it comes *after* the thing: {{บ้านของฉัน|bâan kɔ̌ɔng chǎn}} “house of me” = my house. With family and close things it's usually left out: {{แม่ผม|mɛ̂ɛ pǒm}} “my mom”, {{เพื่อนฉัน|pʉ̂ʉan chǎn}} “my friend”.

**Mine, yours, whose?** {{ของ|kɔ̌ɔng}} + a person, on its own, is “mine, yours…”: {{ของผม|kɔ̌ɔng pǒm}} “mine”, {{ของคุณ|kɔ̌ɔng kun}} “yours”. “Whose?” is {{ของใคร|kɔ̌ɔng krai}}: {{นี่ของใคร|nîi kɔ̌ɔng krai}} “whose is this?”.

**Family words go by age.** Thai has no word for just “brother” or “sister”: it says whether they're older ({{พี่|pîi}}) or younger ({{น้อง|nɔ́ɔng}}). Add {{ชาย|chaai}} “male” or {{สาว|sǎao}} “female” only when you need to: {{พี่ชาย|pîi-chaai}} “older brother”, {{น้องสาว|nɔ́ɔng-sǎao}} “younger sister”. {{พี่น้อง|pîi-nɔ́ɔng}} is “brothers and sisters”.

**Age.** {{อายุ|aa-yú}} “age”, the number, then {{ปี|bpii}} “years”: {{ผมอายุสามสิบปี|pǒm aa-yú sǎam-sìp bpii}} “I'm thirty”. “How old?” is {{อายุเท่าไหร่|aa-yú tâo-rài}}. For a young child, years are {{ขวบ|kùuap}}: {{ห้าขวบ|hâa kùuap}} “five years old”.

blocks.p: **Right now: กำลัง.** Put {{กำลัง|gam-lang}} before the verb to say something is going on at this moment: {{ผมกำลังกิน|pǒm gam-lang gin}} “I'm eating”. Thais often add {{อยู่|yùu}} at the end as well: {{กำลังกินอยู่|gam-lang gin yùu}}. One of the two is enough; both together is very common.

**อยู่ after a verb.** On its own after a verb (or after what follows the verb), {{อยู่|yùu}} also means “in the middle of, still at it”: {{ทำอะไรอยู่|tam à-rai yùu}} “what are you doing?”, {{เขานอนอยู่|kǎo nɔɔn yùu}} “he's asleep”. It's the same {{อยู่|yùu}} as “to be somewhere”: you *are* in that activity.

table: {{อาบน้ำอยู่|àap-náam yùu}}
{{กำลังประชุมอยู่|gam-lang bprà-chum yùu}}

blocks.p: **Asking.** {{ทำอะไรอยู่|tam à-rai yùu}} “what are you doing (right now)?” is the classic phone and message question. Without {{อยู่|yùu}}, {{ทำอะไร|tam à-rai}} can also mean “what do you do?” in general.

**Not only now.** {{กำลัง|gam-lang}} just says “in progress”; the time comes from the rest of the sentence. With a past moment it's “was …ing”: {{ตอนคุณโทรมา ผมกำลังอาบน้ำอยู่|dtɔɔn kun too maa pǒm gam-lang àap náam yùu}} “when you called, I was in the shower”.

blocks.p: **จะ: what's coming.** {{จะ|jà}} goes before the verb to say something is going to happen: {{ผมจะไป|pǒm jà bpai}} “I'll go, I'm going to go”. It covers English “will”, “going to” and “I'm (doing it) tomorrow”.

**With a time word.** {{จะ|jà}} often comes with a time word at the start or the end: {{พรุ่งนี้ผมจะไปตลาด|prûng níi pǒm jà bpai dtà-làat}} “tomorrow I'm going to the market”. Once the time word makes it clear, quick speech may drop {{จะ|jà}}: {{พรุ่งนี้ไปตลาด|prûng níi bpai dtà-làat}}.

table: {{อาทิตย์หน้า|aa-tít nâa}}

blocks.p: **Won't, and asking.** “Won't” is {{จะไม่|jà mâi}}: {{ฉันจะไม่บอกใคร|chǎn jà mâi bɔ̀ɔk krai}} “I won't tell anyone”. To ask: {{จะ…ไหม|jà … mǎi}} “will you…?”, or a question word: {{จะไปไหน|jà bpai nǎi}} “where are you going?”. And a soft “no”: {{ไม่…หรอก|mâi … rɔ̀k}}; {{หรอก|rɔ̀k}} at the end of a negative takes the edge off it.
**หน้า, “front, next”.** After a word for a time, {{หน้า|nâa}} means “next”: {{อาทิตย์หน้า|aa-tít nâa}} “next week”, {{ปีหน้า|bpii nâa}} “next year”.

lessons.title: Say what you can and can't do
lessons.summary: Say what you're able to do, what you know how to do, and what's allowed: Thai has three words for “can”.
lessons.topic: a verb + {{ได้|dâai}} (able, allowed); a verb + {{เป็น|bpen}} (know how to); {{สามารถ|sǎa-mâat}} (formal); {{ไม่ได้|mâi dâai}} and {{ไม่เป็น|mâi bpen}}

goal.t: ผมพูดภาษาไทยได้นิดหน่อยครับ
goal.r: pǒm pûut paa-sǎa tai dâai nít-nɔ̀i kráp
goal.tr: I can speak a little Thai.

dialog.t: คุณพูดภาษาไทยได้ไหมคะ
dialog.r: kun pûut paa-sǎa tai dâai mǎi ká

dialog.t: ได้นิดหน่อยครับ แต่อ่านไม่ได้
dialog.r: dâai nít-nɔ̀i kráp, dtɛ̀ɛ àan mâi dâai
dialog.tr: A little. But I can't read it.

dialog.t: ขับรถเป็นไหมคะ
dialog.r: kàp rót bpen mǎi ká
dialog.tr: Do you know how to drive?

dialog.t: เป็นครับ แต่ที่นี่ผมขับไม่ได้ ไม่มีใบขับขี่
dialog.r: bpen kráp, dtɛ̀ɛ tîi-nîi pǒm kàp mâi dâai, mâi mii bai-kàp-kìi
dialog.tr: Yes. But I can't drive here: I don't have a license.

dialog.t: ว่ายน้ำเป็นไหมคะ
dialog.r: wâai-náam bpen mǎi ká

dialog.t: ไม่เป็นครับ
dialog.r: mâi bpen kráp

blocks.p: **ได้ after the verb.** “Can” goes at the *end*: the verb, what follows it, then {{ได้|dâai}}: {{พูดภาษาไทยได้|pûut paa-sǎa tai dâai}} “speak Thai can”. It means you're able to, it's possible, or it's allowed. “Can't” is {{ไม่ได้|mâi dâai}}, also at the end: {{อ่านไม่ได้|àan mâi dâai}} “can't read (it)”.

**เป็น: know how to.** For a skill you've learned (swimming, driving, cooking, a language), Thais often say the verb + {{เป็น|bpen}}: {{ว่ายน้ำเป็น|wâai náam bpen}} “knows how to swim”, {{ไม่เป็น|mâi bpen}} “never learned how”. Tom's answers show the difference: {{ขับรถเป็น|kàp rót bpen}} “I know how to drive”, but {{ขับไม่ได้|kàp mâi dâai}} “I'm not able to (here)”.

**สามารถ: formal.** {{สามารถ|sǎa-mâat}} goes *before* the verb, usually with {{ได้|dâai}} still at the end: {{สามารถจ่ายด้วยบัตรได้|sǎa-mâat jàai dûai bàt dâai}} “(you) can pay by card”. You'll see it on signs and hear it in announcements more than in conversation.

table: {{ไปไม่ได้|bpai mâi dâai}}
{{ทำอาหารเป็น|tam aa-hǎan bpen}}
{{ทำอาหารไม่เป็น|tam aa-hǎan mâi bpen}}
{{สามารถใช้ได้|sǎa-mâat chái dâai}}

blocks.p: **Asking and answering.** {{…ได้ไหม|… dâai mǎi}} “can you…?” and {{…เป็นไหม|… bpen mǎi}} “do you know how to…?”. The answer is {{ได้|dâai}} / {{ไม่ได้|mâi dâai}}, or {{เป็น|bpen}} / {{ไม่เป็น|mâi bpen}}.

blocks.tip: {{ได้|dâai}} is a busy word. Before a noun it's “get” ({{ได้เงิน|dâai ngən}} “get money”); at the end of a request, “may I” ({{ได้ไหม|dâai mǎi}}); and before a verb it says whether something happened (a later lesson).

lessons.title: Say what you have to and should do
lessons.summary: Say what you have to do, what you don't have to do, what you should do, and what's not allowed.
lessons.topic: {{ต้อง|dtɔ̂ng}} “have to”; {{ไม่ต้อง|mâi dtɔ̂ng}} “don't have to”; {{ควร(จะ)|kuuan (jà)}} “should”; {{ห้าม|hâam}} “not allowed”; {{อย่า|yàa}} “don't”

goal.t: พรุ่งนี้ผมต้องตื่นเช้าครับ
goal.r: prûng-níi pǒm dtɔ̂ng dtʉ̀ʉn cháao kráp
goal.tr: I have to get up early tomorrow.

dialog.t: พรุ่งนี้เราจะไปวัดพระแก้ว ต้องใส่อะไรคะ
dialog.r: prûng-níi rao jà bpai wát prá-gɛ̂ɛo, dtɔ̂ng sài à-rai ká

dialog.tr: You have to wear long pants. Shorts aren't allowed.

dialog.t: ต้องซื้อตั๋วไหมคะ
dialog.r: dtɔ̂ng sʉ́ʉ dtǔua mǎi ká
dialog.tr: Do we have to buy tickets?

dialog.tr: And you should go early: there aren't many people then.

dialog.t: อย่าลืมเตือนฉันนะคะ
dialog.r: yàa lʉʉm dtʉʉan chǎn ná ká

blocks.p: **ต้อง: have to.** {{ต้อง|dtɔ̂ng}} goes before the verb: {{ผมต้องไป|pǒm dtɔ̂ng bpai}} “I have to go”, {{ต้องจ่ายเงินสด|dtɔ̂ng jàai ngən-sòt}} “you have to pay cash”. To ask: {{ต้อง…ไหม|dtɔ̂ng … mǎi}} “do I have to…?”.

**ไม่ต้อง: no need.** {{ไม่ต้อง|mâi dtɔ̂ng}} says it isn't necessary: {{ไม่ต้องจ่าย|mâi dtɔ̂ng jàai}} “you don't have to pay”. On its own it's a friendly “no need”, and {{ไม่ต้องห่วง|mâi dtɔ̂ng hùuang}} is “don't worry”.
**ควร: should.** {{ควร|kuuan}}, or {{ควรจะ|kuuan jà}}, before the verb gives advice: {{คุณควรพักผ่อน|kun kuuan pák pɔ̀n}} “you should rest”. {{ไม่ควร|mâi kuuan}} is “shouldn't”.

**ห้าม and อย่า: don't.** {{ห้าม|hâam}} “it's forbidden to” is for rules and signs: {{ห้ามสูบบุหรี่|hâam sùup bù-rìi}} “no smoking”. {{อย่า|yàa}} “don't” is for telling someone: {{อย่าลืม|yàa lʉʉm}} “don't forget”. {{นะ|ná}} at the end makes it friendly: {{อย่าลืมนะ|yàa lʉʉm ná}}.

{{ไม่ควรไป|mâi kuuan bpai}}

lessons.title: Suggest and invite: let's…
lessons.summary: Invite someone, suggest what to do together, and say yes, or no, politely.
lessons.topic: {{…กันไหม|gan mǎi}} “shall we?”; {{…กันเถอะ|gan tə̀}} “let's”; {{…ดีไหม|dii mǎi}} “how about…?”; question word + {{ดี|dii}}; {{ชวน|chuuan}}

dialog.r: dâai kráp, chuuan fǒn bpai dûai mǎi kráp

dialog.tr: Good idea. See you at six, then.

blocks.p: **กัน: together.** {{กัน|gan}} after a verb means “together, with each other”. Add {{ไหม|mǎi}} and you have an invitation: {{ไปกินข้าวกันไหม|bpai gin kâao gan mǎi}} “shall we go and eat (together)?”.
**Let's.** {{…กันเถอะ|gan tə̀}} is “let's”: {{ไปกันเถอะ|bpai gan tə̀}} “let's go”. {{เถอะ|tə̀}} on its own gently urges someone: {{นอนเถอะ|nɔɔn tə̀}} “go to sleep (you need it)”.

**How about…? ดีไหม.** {{…ดีไหม|dii mǎi}} “is … good?” puts forward an idea: {{ไปทะเลดีไหม|bpai tá-lee dii mǎi}} “how about the beach?”. And {{ดี|dii}} after a question word asks for a choice: {{ไปไหนดี|bpai nǎi dii}} “where shall we go?”, {{กินอะไรดี|gin à-rai dii}} “what shall we eat?”.
**Asking someone along.** {{ชวน|chuuan}} is “invite, ask (someone) to come”: {{ชวนเพื่อนไปด้วย|chuuan pʉ̂ʉan bpai dûai}} “ask a friend along”.

lessons.title: Say what you did: the past without a past tense
lessons.summary: Tell someone what you did yesterday or last weekend. Thai has no past tense: a time word is enough.
lessons.topic: Past time words ({{เมื่อวาน|mʉ̂ʉa-waan}}, {{เมื่อกี้|mʉ̂ʉa-gîi}}, {{อาทิตย์ที่แล้ว|aa-tít tîi-lɛ́ɛo}}, {{…ก่อน|gɔ̀ɔn}}); {{ไป…มา|bpai … maa}} “went (and came back)”; {{ไปไหนมา|bpai nǎi maa}}

goal.t: เมื่อวานฉันไปตลาดน้ำมาค่ะ
goal.r: mʉ̂ʉa-waan chǎn bpai dtà-làat náam maa kâ
goal.tr: Yesterday I went to the floating market.

blocks.p: **No past tense.** Thai verbs don't change for the past ({{ไป|bpai}} is “go” and “went”), so a time word does the work: {{เมื่อวานผมไปตลาด|mʉ̂ʉa waan pǒm bpai dtà-làat}} “yesterday I went to the market”. Once the time is clear, the rest of the story needs no more marking: {{ฉันนั่งเรือ แล้วก็กินก๋วยเตี๋ยว|chǎn nâng rʉʉa lɛ́ɛo gɔ̂ gin gǔai-dtǐao}} “I took a boat and had noodles”.

table: {{อาทิตย์ที่แล้ว|aa-tít tîi-lɛ́ɛo}}
{{สองวันก่อน|sɔ̌ɔng wan gɔ̀ɔn}}

blocks.p: **เมื่อ, ที่แล้ว, ก่อน.** {{เมื่อ|mʉ̂ʉa}} before a time word puts it in the past: {{เมื่อวาน|mʉ̂ʉa-waan}} “yesterday”, {{เมื่อคืน|mʉ̂ʉa-kʉʉn}} “last night”. {{ที่แล้ว|tîi-lɛ́ɛo}} after one means “last”: {{เดือนที่แล้ว|dʉʉan tîi-lɛ́ɛo}} “last month”. A length of time + {{ก่อน|gɔ̀ɔn}} is “… ago”: {{สามปีก่อน|sǎam bpii gɔ̀ɔn}} “three years ago”.

**ไป…มา: been and come back.** Thais love to finish with {{มา|maa}} after {{ไป|bpai}} and a place: {{ไปตลาดมา|bpai dtà-làat maa}} “went to the market (and I'm back)”. The everyday greeting {{ไปไหนมา|bpai nǎi maa}} “where have you been?” is like “what have you been up to?”. {{มา|maa}} also follows something you brought back: {{ซื้อผลไม้มา|sʉ́ʉ pǒn-lá-máai maa}} “bought (and brought back) some fruit”.

blocks.p: **แล้ว: done.** {{แล้ว|lɛ́ɛo}} at the end says something has happened, is over: {{ผมกินแล้ว|pǒm gin lɛ́ɛo}} “I've (already) eaten”, {{ถึงแล้ว|tʉ̌ng lɛ́ɛo}} “we're here (we've arrived)”.

**แล้ว: now changed.** After an adjective, {{แล้ว|lɛ́ɛo}} says something has *become* so: {{หิวแล้ว|hǐu lɛ́ɛo}} “I'm hungry now”, {{ดึกแล้ว|dʉ̀k lɛ́ɛo}} “it's late (now)”. After a verb of happening, it says it has started: {{ฝนตกแล้ว|fǒn dtòk lɛ́ɛo}} “it's raining now”.

**…yet? หรือยัง.** To ask whether something has happened yet, end with {{หรือยัง|rʉ̌ʉ yang}} “or not yet?”: {{กินข้าวหรือยัง|gin kâao rʉ̌ʉ yang}} “have you eaten yet?”. Thais ask this as a kind of “how are you?”. The answers: {{…แล้ว|… lɛ́ɛo}} “yes, I have”, or {{ยัง|yang}} “not yet”.

**ยัง: not yet, still.** {{ยังไม่|yang mâi}} + a verb is “not … yet”; for something you haven't *done* yet, add {{ได้|dâai}}: {{ยังไม่ได้กิน|yang mâi dâai gin}} “I haven't eaten yet”. With {{อยู่|yùu}} at the end, {{ยัง|yang}} means “still”: {{ร้านยังเปิดอยู่|ráan yang bpə̀ət yùu}} “the shop is still open”.

blocks.p: **ไม่ได้ + a verb: didn't.** To say something did *not* happen, put {{ไม่ได้|mâi dâai}} before the verb: {{ผมไม่ได้ไป|pǒm mâi dâai bpai}} “I didn't go”, {{ฉันไม่ได้กินข้าวเช้า|chǎn mâi dâai gin kâao cháao}} “I didn't have breakfast”. Plain {{ไม่|mâi}} before a verb is for habits and decisions: {{ผมไม่ไป|pǒm mâi bpai}} “I'm not going, I won't go”.

table: I'm not going. / I don't go.
{{ผมไม่ได้ไป|pǒm mâi dâai bpai}}
{{ผมไปไม่ได้|pǒm bpai mâi dâai}}
I can't go. / I couldn't go.
{{ผมยังไม่ได้ไป|pǒm yang mâi dâai bpai}}

blocks.p: **Where ได้ goes.** Watch the order: {{ไม่ได้ไป|mâi dâai bpai}}, before the verb, is “didn't go”; {{ไปไม่ได้|bpai mâi dâai}}, after it, is “can't go”. It's one of the trickiest pairs in Thai, and worth saying out loud a few times.

**“Not really”.** {{ไม่ได้|mâi dâai}} also puts a wrong idea right, even about now: {{ผมไม่ได้โกรธ|pǒm mâi dâai gròot}} “I'm not angry (that's not it)”, {{ฉันไม่ได้พูดแบบนั้น|chǎn mâi dâai pûut bɛ̀ɛp nán}} “I didn't say that”.
**Because.** {{เพราะ|prɔ́}}, or {{เพราะว่า|prɔ́ wâa}}, gives the reason, after what happened: {{ผมไม่ได้ไป เพราะฝนตก|pǒm mâi dâai bpai prɔ́ fǒn dtòk}} “I didn't go, because it rained”.

blocks.p: **เคย: ever.** {{เคย|kəəi}} before a verb says you've had that experience at some time: {{ผมเคยไปญี่ปุ่น|pǒm kəəi bpai yîi-bpùn}} “I've been to Japan”. {{ไม่เคย|mâi kəəi}} is “never”: {{ฉันไม่เคยขี่ช้าง|chǎn mâi kəəi kìi cháang}} “I've never ridden an elephant”.
**Asking.** {{เคย…ไหม|kəəi … mǎi}} is “have you ever…?”. Answer {{เคย|kəəi}} or {{ไม่เคย|mâi kəəi}}: as always, the verb word from the question.

**How many times.** {{ครั้ง|kráng}} “time, occasion” is the classifier: {{สองครั้ง|sɔ̌ɔng kráng}} “twice”, {{หลายครั้ง|lǎai kráng}} “many times”, {{ครั้งแรก|kráng rɛ̂ɛk}} “the first time”. “How many times?” is {{กี่ครั้ง|gìi kráng}}.

**เคย: used to.** For a past habit, {{เคย|kəəi}} means “used to”: {{ผมเคยอยู่เชียงใหม่|pǒm kəəi yùu chiiang-mài}} “I used to live in Chiang Mai (I don't now)”. The situation tells you which it is: an experience, or a habit that's over.

lessons.title: Say how long and since when
lessons.summary: Say how long you've lived here, studied Thai or been waiting, and since when.
lessons.topic: a verb + {{มา|maa}} + a length of time + {{แล้ว|lɛ́ɛo}}; {{ตั้งแต่|dtâng-dtɛ̀ɛ}} “since”; {{นานแค่ไหน|naan kɛ̂ɛ nǎi}}, {{กี่ปีแล้ว|gìi bpii lɛ́ɛo}}

goal.t: ผมเรียนภาษาไทยมาสองปีแล้วครับ
goal.r: pǒm riian paa-sǎa tai maa sɔ̌ɔng bpii lɛ́ɛo kráp
goal.tr: I've been learning Thai for two years.

dialog.t: คุณอยู่เมืองไทยมานานแค่ไหนแล้วคะ
dialog.r: kun yùu mʉʉang tai maa naan kɛ̂ɛ nǎi lɛ́ɛo ká
dialog.tr: How long have you lived in Thailand?

dialog.t: สามปีแล้วครับ ตั้งแต่เรียนจบ
dialog.r: sǎam bpii lɛ́ɛo kráp, dtâng-dtɛ̀ɛ riian jòp

dialog.t: พูดภาษาไทยเก่งนะคะ เรียนมานานไหมคะ
dialog.r: pûut paa-sǎa tai gèng ná ká, riian maa naan mǎi ká
dialog.tr: Your Thai is good! Have you been learning long?

dialog.t: สองปีแล้วครับ แต่ยังพูดไม่ค่อยเก่ง
dialog.r: sɔ̌ɔng bpii lɛ́ɛo kráp, dtɛ̀ɛ yang pûut mâi kɔ̂i gèng
dialog.tr: Two years. But I still don't speak very well.

blocks.p: **How long, up to now.** For something that started in the past and is still going on, Thai says the verb, then {{มา|maa}} “come (up to now)”, the length of time, and {{แล้ว|lɛ́ɛo}}: {{ผมอยู่ที่นี่มาห้าปีแล้ว|pǒm yùu tîi nîi maa hâa bpii lɛ́ɛo}} “I've lived here for five years”. English needs “have been” for this; Thai just needs {{มา…แล้ว|maa … lɛ́ɛo}}.

**Asking how long.** {{นานแค่ไหน|naan kɛ̂ɛ nǎi}} is “how long”; or ask with the unit: {{กี่ปีแล้ว|gìi bpii lɛ́ɛo}} “how many years (now)?”, {{กี่วันแล้ว|gìi wan lɛ́ɛo}} “how many days?”. {{นานไหม|naan mǎi}} is “(has it been) long?”.
**Since.** {{ตั้งแต่|dtâng-dtɛ̀ɛ}} “since, from” + a time or an event: {{ตั้งแต่เมื่อวาน|dtâng-dtɛ̀ɛ mʉ̂ʉa waan}} “since yesterday”, {{ตั้งแต่เด็ก|dtâng-dtɛ̀ɛ dèk}} “since (I was) a child”.

ex.t: ฉันรอมาครึ่งชั่วโมงแล้วค่ะ
ex.r: chǎn rɔɔ maa krʉ̂ng chûua-moong lɛ́ɛo kâ
ex.tr: I've been waiting for half an hour.

ex.t: เขาทำงานที่นี่มาสิบปีแล้วครับ
ex.r: kǎo tam-ngaan tîi-nîi maa sìp bpii lɛ́ɛo kráp
ex.tr: He's worked here for ten years.

ex.t: เราแต่งงานกันมาห้าปีแล้วค่ะ
ex.r: rao dtɛ̀ng-ngaan gan maa hâa bpii lɛ́ɛo kâ
ex.tr: We've been married for five years.

ex.t: ฝนตกตั้งแต่เมื่อคืนครับ
ex.r: fǒn dtòk dtâng-dtɛ̀ɛ mʉ̂ʉa-kʉʉn kráp
ex.tr: It's been raining since last night.

ex.t: ฉันชอบวาดรูปตั้งแต่เด็กค่ะ
ex.r: chǎn chɔ̂ɔp wâat rûup dtâng-dtɛ̀ɛ dèk kâ
ex.tr: I've loved drawing since I was a child.

ex.t: คุณรู้จักเขามานานแค่ไหนแล้วครับ
ex.r: kun rúu-jàk kǎo maa naan kɛ̂ɛ nǎi lɛ́ɛo kráp
ex.tr: How long have you known her?

ex.t: ไม่ได้เจอกันนานเลยนะคะ
ex.r: mâi dâai jəə gan naan ləəi ná ká
ex.note: “(we) haven't met for a long time”

blocks.tip: {{ไม่ได้เจอกันนาน|mâi dâai jəə gan naan}} “we haven't met for a long time” is the Thai “long time no see”. There's {{ไม่ได้|mâi dâai}} again: something that hasn't happened.

mistakes.wrong: ผมอยู่ที่นี่ห้าปีครับ
mistakes.right: ผมอยู่ที่นี่มาห้าปีแล้วครับ
mistakes.tr: I've lived here for five years.
mistakes.why: Without {{มา…แล้ว|maa … lɛ́ɛo}} it can sound like five years you will stay, or stayed once. {{มา…แล้ว|maa … lɛ́ɛo}} says “up to now”.

mistakes.wrong: ผมเรียนแล้วมาสองปีครับ
mistakes.right: ผมเรียนมาสองปีแล้วครับ
mistakes.tr: I've been learning for two years.
mistakes.why: The order is: the verb, {{มา|maa}}, the time, {{แล้ว|lɛ́ɛo}}.

{{ตั้งแต่ฝนตกเมื่อคืน|dtâng-dtɛ̀ɛ fǒn dtòk mʉ̂ʉa-kʉʉn}}

answers.r: pǒm riian paa-sǎa tai maa hòk dʉʉan lɛ́ɛo kráp, pǒm yùu bâan níi maa sìp bpii lɛ́ɛo

answers.r: chǎn riian paa-sǎa tai maa sǎam dʉʉan lɛ́ɛo kâ, yùu tîi-nîi dtâng-dtɛ̀ɛ bpii tîi-lɛ́ɛo
answers.tr: I've been learning Thai for three months. I've lived here since last year.

lessons.title: Tell a story in order
lessons.summary: Tell what happened, step by step: first, then, after that, and what was going on when it happened.
lessons.topic: {{ตอนแรก|dtɔɔn rɛ̂ɛk}}, {{แล้วก็|lɛ́ɛo-gɔ̂}}, {{หลังจากนั้น|lǎng-jàak nán}}, {{สุดท้าย|sùt-táai}}; {{ตอนที่|dtɔɔn tîi}} “when”; {{กำลัง…อยู่|gam-lang … yùu}} for the background; {{ก็เลย|gɔ̂ ləəi}} “so”

goal.t: ตอนที่ฉันกำลังเดินกลับบ้าน ฝนก็ตกลงมาค่ะ
goal.r: dtɔɔn tîi chǎn gam-lang dəən glàp bâan, fǒn gɔ̂ dtòk long maa kâ
goal.tr: I was walking home when it started to rain.

dialog.t: เมื่อวานเป็นยังไงบ้างคะ
dialog.r: mʉ̂ʉa-waan bpen yang-ngai bâng ká

dialog.t: แย่มากค่ะ ตอนแรกฉันไปตลาด ซื้อผักกับผลไม้
dialog.r: yɛ̂ɛ mâak kâ, dtɔɔn rɛ̂ɛk chǎn bpai dtà-làat, sʉ́ʉ pàk gàp pǒn-lá-máai
dialog.tr: Awful! First I went to the market and bought vegetables and fruit.

dialog.t: หลังจากนั้นก็ไปรอรถเมล์ ตอนที่กำลังรอ ฉันเห็นว่ากระเป๋าเงินหายไป
dialog.r: lǎng-jàak nán gɔ̂ bpai rɔɔ rót-mee, dtɔɔn tîi gam-lang rɔɔ, chǎn hěn wâa grà-bpǎo ngən hǎai bpai
dialog.tr: After that I went to wait for the bus. While I was waiting, I saw my wallet was gone.

dialog.t: ตายแล้ว แล้วทำยังไงคะ
dialog.r: dtaai lɛ́ɛo, lɛ́ɛo tam yang-ngai ká
dialog.tr: Oh no! So what did you do?

dialog.t: ฉันก็เลยวิ่งกลับไปที่ตลาด สุดท้ายแม่ค้าเก็บไว้ให้ค่ะ
dialog.r: chǎn gɔ̂ ləəi wîng glàp bpai tîi dtà-làat, sùt-táai mɛ̂ɛ-káa gèp wái hâi kâ
dialog.tr: So I ran back to the market. In the end the stall owner had kept it for me.

blocks.p: **Putting it in order.** A story moves on with little linking words: {{ตอนแรก|dtɔɔn rɛ̂ɛk}} “at first”, {{แล้วก็|lɛ́ɛo-gɔ̂}} “and then”, {{หลังจากนั้น|lǎng-jàak nán}} “after that”, {{สุดท้าย|sùt-táai}} “in the end”. The verbs stay as they are: the past is clear from the start of the story.

table: {{หลังจากนั้น|lǎng-jàak nán}}
{{ก่อนหน้านั้น|gɔ̀ɔn nâa nán}}

blocks.p: **When: ตอนที่.** {{ตอนที่|dtɔɔn tîi}} “at the time that” + a sentence sets the scene: {{ตอนที่ฉันกลับถึงบ้าน|dtɔɔn tîi chǎn glàp tʉ̌ng bâan}} “when I got home”. The main event follows, often with {{ก็|gɔ̂}} “then”: {{ตอนที่ฉันกลับถึงบ้าน ทุกคนก็หลับแล้ว|dtɔɔn tîi chǎn glàp tʉ̌ng bâan túk kon gɔ̂ làp lɛ́ɛo}} “when I got home, everyone was already asleep”.

**The background.** What was going on at the time takes {{กำลัง…อยู่|gam-lang … yùu}}, as in lesson 21: {{ตอนที่ผมกำลังอาบน้ำอยู่ โทรศัพท์ก็ดัง|dtɔɔn tîi pǒm gam-lang àap náam yùu too-rá-sàp gɔ̂ dang}} “I was in the shower when the phone rang”.

**So: ก็เลย.** {{ก็เลย|gɔ̂ ləəi}} “so, and so” gives the result: {{ฝนตก ผมก็เลยไม่ได้ไป|fǒn-dtòk pǒm gɔ̂ ləəi mâi dâai bpai}} “it rained, so I didn't go”. Reasons and results come back in a later lesson.

ex.t: ตอนแรกผมไม่ชอบอาหารเผ็ด แต่ตอนนี้ชอบมากครับ
ex.r: dtɔɔn rɛ̂ɛk pǒm mâi chɔ̂ɔp aa-hǎan pèt, dtɛ̀ɛ dtɔɔn-níi chɔ̂ɔp mâak kráp
ex.tr: At first I didn't like spicy food, but now I love it.

ex.t: เรากินข้าว แล้วก็ไปดูหนังค่ะ
ex.r: rao gin kâao, lɛ́ɛo-gɔ̂ bpai duu nǎng kâ
ex.tr: We ate, and then went to a movie.

ex.t: หลังจากนั้นเขาก็กลับบ้านครับ
ex.r: lǎng-jàak nán kǎo gɔ̂ glàp bâan kráp

ex.t: ตอนที่ฉันกลับถึงบ้าน ทุกคนก็หลับแล้วค่ะ
ex.r: dtɔɔn tîi chǎn glàp tʉ̌ng bâan, túk kon gɔ̂ làp lɛ́ɛo kâ
ex.tr: When I got home, everyone was already asleep.

ex.t: ตอนที่ผมกำลังอาบน้ำอยู่ โทรศัพท์ก็ดังครับ
ex.r: dtɔɔn tîi pǒm gam-lang àap-náam yùu, too-rá-sàp gɔ̂ dang kráp
ex.tr: I was in the shower when the phone rang.

ex.t: สุดท้ายเราก็หาโรงแรมได้ค่ะ
ex.r: sùt-táai rao gɔ̂ hǎa roong-rɛɛm dâai kâ
ex.tr: In the end we managed to find a hotel.

blocks.tip: Thais react to a story with {{จริงเหรอ|jing rə̌ə}} “really?”, {{แล้วไงต่อ|lɛ́ɛo ngai dtɔ̀ɔ}} “and then what?”, or {{ตายแล้ว|dtaai lɛ́ɛo}} “oh no!” (literally “dead already”).

mistakes.wrong: เมื่อวานผมไปแล้วตลาด
mistakes.right: เมื่อวานผมไปตลาด
mistakes.tr: Yesterday I went to the market.
mistakes.why: {{แล้ว|lɛ́ɛo}} isn't a past tense. {{เมื่อวาน|mʉ̂ʉa-waan}} already says it's past; {{แล้ว|lɛ́ɛo}} between the verb and the place makes no sense.

practice.q: Choose the linking word: {{หลังจากนั้น|lǎng-jàak nán}} “after that” or {{ตอนแรก|dtɔɔn rɛ̂ɛk}} “at first”.
practice.t: เรากินข้าว ___ก็ไปเดินเล่นค่ะ
practice.tr: We ate. After that we went for a walk.
options: หลังจากนั้น
ตอนแรก
practice.why: The next step of the story: {{หลังจากนั้น|lǎng-jàak nán}}.

practice.q: “I was walking home when it started to rain.” Which part takes {{กำลัง|gam-lang}}?
options: walking home: the background
it started to rain: the event
both parts
practice.why: {{กำลัง|gam-lang}} is for what was going on; the event that happened in the middle of it gets {{ก็|gɔ̂}}.

practice.q: Put the words in order.
practice.tr: When I got home, everyone was already asleep. (a woman speaking)
words: กลับถึงบ้าน

practice.q: Nok asks about your day at the beach. Choose your replies (you're a man).

lines.t: เมื่อวานไปไหนมาคะ

options: ไปทะเลมาครับ ตอนแรกว่ายน้ำ แล้วก็กินอาหารทะเล
ไปทะเลมาครับ แล้วก็ตอนแรกว่ายน้ำ
lines.why: {{ตอนแรก|dtɔɔn rɛ̂ɛk}} begins the story; {{แล้วก็|lɛ́ɛo-gɔ̂}} moves it on.

lines.t: แล้วไงต่อคะ

options: สุดท้ายก็กลับบ้านตอนดึกครับ
สุดท้ายจะกลับบ้านตอนดึกครับ
lines.why: It's the end of a past story: no {{จะ|jà}}.

practice.q: You're a man. Say “I was in the shower when the phone rang.”
practice.answer: ตอนที่ผมกำลังอาบน้ำอยู่ โทรศัพท์ก็ดังครับ
practice.r: dtɔɔn tîi pǒm gam-lang àap-náam yùu, too-rá-sàp gɔ̂ dang kráp

practice.q: Your turn: tell what happened on a day you remember, in three steps: first, then, in the end.

answers.t: ตอนแรกผมไปสนามบินครับ แล้วก็รอเครื่องบินสามชั่วโมง สุดท้ายก็ถึงเชียงใหม่ตอนเที่ยงคืน
answers.r: dtɔɔn rɛ̂ɛk pǒm bpai sà-nǎam-bin kráp, lɛ́ɛo-gɔ̂ rɔɔ krʉ̂ʉang-bin sǎam chûua-moong, sùt-táai gɔ̂ tʉ̌ng chiiang-mài dtɔɔn tîiang-kʉʉn
answers.tr: First I went to the airport, then I waited three hours for the plane. In the end I got to Chiang Mai at midnight.

answers.t: ตอนแรกฉันหลงทางค่ะ แล้วก็ถามตำรวจ สุดท้ายก็หาโรงแรมเจอ
answers.r: dtɔɔn rɛ̂ɛk chǎn lǒng taang kâ, lɛ́ɛo-gɔ̂ tǎam dtam-rùuat, sùt-táai gɔ̂ hǎa roong-rɛɛm jəə
answers.tr: At first I got lost, then I asked a police officer, and in the end I found the hotel.
